leaveOut.why: 28 of its 57 traced buildings fall on the Capitol Square lawn, a public square since the Capitol was built (https://vga.virginia.gov/?p=73), so the sheet's fit (read by eye) is wrong; its other buildings are taken to be out of place too. Left out until the sheet is placed again.
3 of its 5 traced buildings fall on the Capitol Square lawn: the same misfit as sheet 5.

Buildings of the downtown tracing taken from volume 1's small-scale key map (1924-25) whose centers fall in the blocks traced from the 1925 volume 3 sheets (Leigh Street north, and Clay to Leigh from 1st to 7th Streets). At that scale they are coarse and several are misplaced: one, drawn as a six-story fireproof block of 4,222 m2, covers the Leigh Street Memorial M.E. Church, the Salvation Army home and their neighbors on sheet 309; others fall on yards or a street. Before 1952 the volume 3 sheets draw these blocks instead (tools/sanborn/jw/life25.py); from 1952 on they are as before.

ground.name: Ramp banks at the I-64 junction, before 1955
ground.note: Estimate. East of 1st Street the interchange ramps stand on the old plateau rim above Shockoe Valley. The USGS Richmond sheet surveyed 1933-34 shows ground there at about the height the lidar measures today (its 150-foot contour, labeled near the valley rim, falls where today's does), so the ground is kept as measured, except that banks narrower than 50 m (the ramps' embankments, up to 9 m high) are taken down to the ground beside them. The ravine the sheet shows heading into the plateau north of the junction, and the valley side under I-95 south of it, are not rebuilt: the lidar is kept there.

ground.note: Estimate, not a survey. The Richmond-Petersburg Turnpike (1955-58) runs through the ward in a trench up to about 8 m deep (3 to 6.5 m where the old cross streets ran). Inside this outline the lidar is set aside and the ground rebuilt as the smoothest surface (a membrane) that meets the measured ground at the outline and carries each street listed here through at grade, straight between its surviving ends. The outline is today's motorway and ramp ways (OpenStreetMap) buffered 22 m (10 m for ramps), widened over the cut slopes the lidar shows (slopes over 12% within 60 m of a motorway), and simplified; east of 1st and Duval streets it keeps only the main line (30 m either side). Checked by moving the outline onto undisturbed plateau nearby (0.3-1.1 m RMS) and against the USGS Richmond sheet surveyed 1933-34 (10-foot contours: no contour can be read near seven points along the trench, and the rebuilt ground would move at most 0.8 m to agree). Error about 1.5 m (95%) mid-trench, 3 m at its ends; a small ravine the sheet shows near 7th Street is not rebuilt (ground.md in the story folder).

title: Richmond in 1937, as the Home Owners' Loan Corporation graded it
about: In 1937 the federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation graded Richmond's residential areas from A to D. The redlining story draws its grades on the ground, with the buildings standing then.

epochs.title: The HOLC's grades
epochs.note: Buildings standing today that the city dates to 1937 or before, and the series' curated features; the grades from the 1937 map (outlines.py names the outline set).

epochs.title: Today, over the 1937 grades
epochs.note: Today's buildings and streets, with the 1937 grades under them.

features.name: Westhampton line
features.note: West on Floyd Avenue from Robinson Street to the belt line railroad, under it in a tunnel, then a little north to Grove Avenue; out Grove to Three Chopt Road; then on its own right-of-way beside Three Chopt to Towana Road, and on (the line of today's Campus Drive) to Westhampton Park, which became the University of Richmond's campus in 1914. The right-of-way beside Three Chopt is drawn down the strip between today's road and the frontage street beside it, halfway between them: approximate.

features.name: Belmont line
features.route: Broad Street – Sheppard Street – Cary Street – Belmont Avenue
features.note: The Broad Street line's extension west from Robinson Street to Sheppard, south to Cary, later carried on eleven blocks to Garrett Street. Which street carried the last stretch is read from the 1925 plate's 'Belmont' label.

features.name: Broad Street line
features.route: Broad Street, Sheppard Street to Church Hill
features.note: Broad Street, the spine of the system, from the Belmont line's turn at Sheppard Street east to Church Hill. The east end is approximate.

features.name: State Fair Grounds spur
features.route: Boulevard north to the Fair Grounds
features.note: The 1925 plate shows a short spur north from Broad Street ending in a loop. It is drawn here up the Boulevard to the State Fair Grounds (1906–1941, on the site of The Diamond); which street the spur took is not certain.

features.name: Main Street line
features.route: Main Street, Robinson Street to Shockoe
features.note: West Main Street, which the line turned into a commercial street through the Fan, east to Shockoe. The west end is approximate.

features.name: Harrison Street line
features.note: A crosstown link on Harrison Street between the Main, Floyd and Broad lines, as the 1925 plate shows it.

features.name: Reservoir (Byrd) Park line
features.note: Down Robinson Street to Reservoir Park (Byrd Park), one of the trolley's favorite destinations, along Lakeview Avenue as the 1925 plate labels it. Lakeview Avenue is mapped today only to Shields Lake; the last 450 m, to the end of the line, are drawn straight and are approximate.

features.name: Clay Street line
features.note: Sprague's first line of 1888 ran from Church Hill to Clay and Hancock Streets; the 1925 plate still shows Clay Street. The ends are approximate.

features.name: Brookland and Lakeside line
features.route: 1st Street – North Avenue – Brookland Park – Chamberlayne – Laburnum – Hermitage Road
features.note: Over the First Street viaduct (1891) into Barton Heights, then west along Brookland Park Boulevard, north up the median of Chamberlayne Avenue, west on Laburnum and north on Hermitage Road to Lakeside Park and Lewis Ginter's Lakeside Wheel Club. The run beyond Hermitage Road along Lakeside Avenue is approximate. OSM maps Monteiro Street with a gap north of Lakewood Street; the line is drawn straight across it.

features.name: Highland Park line
features.route: 5th Street – Northside Viaduct – Highland Park loop
features.note: North on Fifth Street over the Northside Viaduct (opened in 1891, an iron bridge 1,200 feet long) to Chestnut Hill and Highland Park, and after 1908 round a loop by Meadowbridge Road, Milton Street and Highland Street (the cross street joining them, Second Avenue here, is approximate). The Hull Street–Highland Park line was Richmond's last: the last car ran on 25 November 1949. Fifth Street is drawn straight across today's interstate, as it ran then.

features.name: Marshall Street line (Fulton)
features.route: Marshall Street Viaduct – Church Hill – Fulton
features.note: Across Shockoe Valley on the Marshall Street Viaduct (1911, since demolished: drawn straight) from College Street to 21st Street at Jefferson Park, out Marshall Street, and down to Fulton along Williamsburg Avenue. The route from Marshall Street down to Fulton is approximate. Along Williamsburg Avenue in front of the Armitage Manufacturing Company's building (1900) the line is drawn on the avenue's far side, clear of the wall: approximate.

features.name: Venable Street line
features.route: 17th Street – Venable Street – 25th Street – Nine Mile Road
features.note: North on 17th Street, east along Venable Street through Union Hill, and up 25th Street to Nine Mile Road, the road the Seven Pines line took out of the city (chartered along 25th to 29th Streets and Nine Mile Road). The federal government bought the Seven Pines line in 1918 for a wartime plant; how far cars ran out Nine Mile Road in 1925 is not certain.

features.name: Jefferson Avenue line
features.note: Up 21st Street and out Jefferson Avenue past Jefferson Park, one of the trolley's pleasure grounds, as the 1925 plate shows it.

features.name: Hull Street line
features.note: Over the Mayo Bridge into Manchester and out Hull Street. Its last car, No. 408 on the Hull Street–Highland Park run, ended Richmond's streetcars on 25 November 1949. The outer end is approximate.

features.name: Forest Hill line
features.route: 7th Street – Free Bridge – Semmes Avenue – Forest Hill Avenue
features.note: South over the river (the free bridge at Ninth Street), down the median of Semmes Avenue through Woodland Heights, and out Forest Hill Avenue to Forest Hill Park and its amusement park, the most popular trolley destination of all. VEPCO proposed taking up the Semmes Avenue tracks in 1933.

features.name: Richmond–Ashland Railway
features.route: Broad and Laurel – Brook Road – Ashland
features.note: The interurban to Ashland, built as the Richmond and Chesapeake Bay Railway (1907) and run as the Richmond–Ashland Railway from 1919 to 1938: from its terminal at Broad and Laurel Streets (814 West Broad), where the cars left from the second floor, north on a half-mile concrete viaduct over the Seaboard's tracks to just south of Brook Road (drawn straight, its line approximate), then beside Brook Road and on to Ashland on its own right-of-way.
